rules.title: Electricians working for a C-10 contractor must be DIR-certified
rules.plain_english: Anyone who does electrical work as an electrician for a C-10 electrical contractor must hold a state electrician certification (or be a registered apprentice or registered electrician trainee). Uncertified people may not do electrical work that requires certification. The rule follows the employer's license: it covers C-10 contractors only.

alternatives_to_certification: registered electrician trainee under supervision (LC 108.4; 8 CCR 296.3)
parameters.certifying_agency: DIR Labor Commissioner's Office (DLSE) Electrician Certification Unit

rules.title: Who counts as an 'electrician': connections of 100 volt-amperes or more for a C-10
rules.plain_english: 'Electrician' means anyone who connects electrical devices for a C-10 electrical contractor. Connections under 100 volt-amperes are not covered. Also excluded: utility work covered by B&P 7042.5, work normally done by stationary engineers, and temporary or portable equipment run by technicians in theater, film, TV, hotel, exhibition or trade-show work.

excluded_work: public utility work to which B&P 7042.5 applies
electrical work ordinarily and customarily performed by stationary engineers
temporary or portable electrical equipment work by technicians in the theatrical, motion picture production, television, hotel, exhibition or trade show industries

rules.applies_to: Workers doing electrical work (connections of 100 volt-amperes or more) for a CSLB class C-10 electrical contractor, and the C-10 contractors who employ them
rules.citation: Labor Code 108(c) (as quoted by DIR); 8 CCR 290.0
rules.source_location: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/ecu/ECU_FAQ.htm ('Who is required to be certified?' - Labor Code section 108 (c)); also https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/290_0.html
rules.verbatim_quote: As used in this section, "electricians" includes all persons who engage in the connection of electrical devices for electrical contractors licensed pursuant to Section 7058 of the Business and Professions Code, specifically, contractors classified as electrical contractors in the Contractors' State License Board Rules and Regulations. This section does not apply to electrical connections under 100 volt-amperes.

FAQ short answer: 'All electricians who make connections of greater than 100 volt amps who work for C-10 Contractors.' FAQ also says a foreman who sometimes works with the tools must be certified. A September 2026 CSLB board analysis paraphrases the threshold as 'over 100 volts'; the statute and 8 CCR 290.0 say volt-amperes. Only employees of C-10 licensed contractors are covered; electricians employed directly by a school district or plant are not (FAQ).

rules.title: No electrician certification needed for C-7 or C-45 scope work
rules.plain_english: Workers doing work for a C-7 (low voltage systems) or C-45 (electric sign) contractor do not need electrician certification as long as the work stays within the C-7 or C-45 license scope (including incidental and supplemental work), even if the same company also holds a C-10 license.

rules.verbatim_quote: (2) Certification is not required for persons performing work for contractors licensed as class C-7 low voltage systems or class C-45 electric sign contractors as long as the work performed is within the scope of the class C-7 or class C-45 license, including incidental and supplemental work as defined in Section 7059 of the Business and Professions Code, and regardless of whether the same contractor is also licensed as a class C-10 contractor.
rules.notes: Same text quoted on DIR ECU FAQ. Work outside the C-7/C-45 scope for a C-10 contractor still needs certification.

rules.title: Utility high-voltage transmission and distribution workers are exempt
rules.plain_english: Workers on high-voltage transmission or distribution systems owned by a utility do not need electrician certification when they are employed by the utility or by a licensed contractor that mainly installs or maintains transmission or distribution systems.

parameters.exempt_system: high-voltage electrical transmission or distribution system owned by a utility (PUC 224.3, 218, 205, 204)
exempt_employers: licensed contractor principally engaged in installing or maintaining transmission or distribution systems

rules.title: Registered electrical apprentices are exempt; may test in the last year
rules.plain_english: Registered apprentices doing electrical work in a state- or federally-approved apprenticeship program do not need certification. An apprentice within one year of finishing may take the certification exam and becomes certified as soon as the apprenticeship ends. The C-10 contractor must still supervise apprentices properly.

parameters.certified_upon: completion of apprenticeship term after passing exam
approved_programs: state program authorized by federal Office of Apprenticeship

rules.applies_to: Workers doing electrical work (connections of 100 volt-amperes or more) for a CSLB class C-10 electrical contractor, and the C-10 contractors who employ them
rules.verbatim_quote: An apprentice who is within one year of completion of his or her term of apprenticeship shall be permitted to take the certification examination and, upon passing the examination, shall be certified immediately upon completion of the term of apprenticeship.
rules.notes: Willful failure to supervise apprentices is a separate CSLB discipline ground (LC 108.2(h)(3)). Registered apprentices are not counted as uncertified persons for the trainee supervision ratio (8 CCR 296.3(a)).

rules.title: Only the C-10 qualifying person is exempt; partners, officers and C-10 holders working as employees are not
rules.plain_english: The person who qualifies the C-10 license (the one who passed the CSLB exam) may do electrical work for that company and supervise trainees without state electrician certification. Partners or officers who are not the qualifier must be certified, and a C-10 license holder working as an employee under another C-10 contractor's license must be certified.
rules.applies_to: C-10 contractors, their qualifiers, officers, partners and employees
rules.verbatim_quote: (g) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), the qualifying person for a class C-10 electrical contractor license issued by the Contractors' State License Board need not also be certified pursuant to Section 108 to perform electrical work for that licensed contractor or to supervise an uncertified person employed by that licensed contractor pursuant to Section 108.4.
rules.notes: DIR FAQ: 'Only the qualifying person, (meaning the person who took the contractor's license examination), may perform electrical work under that license without a state electrician certificate. Partners and officers of the company who did not sit for the licensing exam, must obtain State Electrician Certification to perform work for which certification is required.' and 'Note that if you are a licensed C-10 contractor but working under another C-10 contractor's license as an employee you must be certified.'

rules.title: Five electrician certification types; General covers all
rules.plain_english: DIR issues five certifications: General Electrician, Residential Electrician, Voice Data Video Technician, Fire/Life Safety Technician and Nonresidential Lighting Technician. Each lets the holder do certified work within that category. A General Electrician certification covers work in all categories.
rules.applies_to: Workers doing electrical work (connections of 100 volt-amperes or more) for a CSLB class C-10 electrical contractor, and the C-10 contractors who employ them
rules.verbatim_quote: (a) An applicant may apply for certification as a General Electrician, a Residential Electrician, a Voice Data Video Technician, a Fire/Life Safety Technician or a Nonresidential Lighting Technician.
rules.notes: 8 CCR 291.0(b): 'Certification as a General Electrician allows one to lawfully perform work for which certification is required in all categories.' Labor Code 108.2(c) requires DIR to maintain these separate certifications. The gap list's 'Voltage Data Signal' label is DIR's 'Voice Data Video Technician'.

rules.title: Residential Electrician scope: dwellings served at 120/208 or 120/240 V
rules.plain_english: A Residential Electrician may work on homes and multifamily buildings (including hotels and motels) whose main use is residential and whose utility service is no more than 3-phase, 4-wire 120/208 or 120/240 volts. They may install panels and feeders for commercial tenant space only if under 50% of the first floor is commercial, may not do the tenant improvements, and may not work in NEC Article 517 (health care) occupancies.
rules.applies_to: Residential Electrician certificate holders and the C-10 contractors who assign them work
rules.verbatim_quote: performs work for a C-10 electrical contractor installing, constructing, or maintaining any electrical system that is covered by the National Electrical Code in single family homes and multi family units, including hotels and motels, where the primary occupancy of the building is considered residential and the maximum voltage received from a utility company is a 3 phase, 4 wire, 120/208 or 120/240 volts.
rules.notes: 8 CCR 290.1 references the 1999 National Electrical Code for article numbers.

rules.title: Scopes of Fire/Life Safety, Voice Data Video and Nonresidential Lighting technicians
rules.plain_english: Fire/Life Safety Technicians work on NEC Article 760 (fire alarm) systems. Voice Data Video Technicians work on systems under NEC Articles 725, 770 (non-composite cables), 800 (non-hybrid cables), 810 and 820. Nonresidential Lighting Technicians repair, service and maintain existing nonresidential lighting fixtures and install retrofit fixtures; they may not install or alter branch circuits, except reconnecting to existing power within 3 feet.

rules.title: Certification application and exam fee: $175 ($75 + $100)
rules.plain_english: Applying for electrician certification costs $75 plus $100 for the exam, $175 total. The fees are not refunded once your application is accepted, and missing your test date forfeits them. If DIR finds the application deficient or short on proof of experience, it returns the application and refunds all fees. Each retake costs another $100.
